apa: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. Sage.
annotation: Origin of the trustworthiness framework (credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability). Cite when justifying rigor criteria as an alternative to validity/reliability.

apa: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2020). Qualitative data analysis: A methods sourcebook (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The standard sourcebook for displays, matrices, and within-/cross-case analysis. Cite for systematic data management and visualization.

apa: Saldaña, J. (2021). The coding manual for qualitative researchers (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The reference catalogue of first- and second-cycle coding methods. Cite to name and justify a specific coding technique.

apa: Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The discovery of grounded theory: Strategies for qualitative research. Aldine. (Routledge reprint, 2017)
annotation: The founding statement of grounded theory and constant comparison. DOI applies to the Routledge reprint. Cite for the origins of inductive theory-building.

apa: Corbin, J., & Strauss, A. (2015). Basics of qualitative research: Techniques and procedures for developing grounded theory (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The systematic/procedural strand of grounded theory (open/axial/selective coding). Cite for structured coding paradigms.

apa: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing grounded theory (2nd ed.). Sage.
annotation: The constructivist reframing of grounded theory. Cite when foregrounding co-construction and researcher reflexivity.

apa: Patton, M. Q. (2015). Qualitative research & evaluation methods (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: Comprehensive reference on purposeful sampling and evaluation-oriented design. Cite for sampling logic and applied contexts.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101.
annotation: The field-defining six-phase thematic analysis paper. The default citation for any thematic analysis.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597.
annotation: Introduces "reflexive TA" and distinguishes it from coding-reliability TA. Cite to specify the reflexive variant.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2021). One size fits all? What counts as quality practice in (reflexive) thematic analysis? Qualitative Research in Psychology, 18(3), 328–352.
annotation: Quality criteria for reflexive TA and a critique of misapplications. Cite when defending TA quality.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2022). Thematic analysis: A practical guide. Sage.
annotation: The definitive practical manual for reflexive TA. Cite for step-by-step procedure.

apa: Timmermans, S., & Tavory, I. (2012). Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis. Sociological Theory, 30(3), 167–186.
annotation: The seminal argument that abduction, not pure induction, drives theory construction. Cite to justify an abductive stance.

apa: Tavory, I., & Timmermans, S. (2014). Abductive analysis: Theorizing qualitative research. University of Chicago Press.
annotation: Book-length treatment of abductive analysis. Cite for the full methodology.

apa: Thomas, D. R. (2006). A general inductive approach for analyzing qualitative evaluation data. American Journal of Evaluation, 27(2), 237–246.
annotation: The canonical statement of the "general inductive approach." Cite for a pragmatic inductive coding workflow.

apa: Hsieh, H.-F., & Shannon, S. E. (2005). Three approaches to qualitative content analysis. Qualitative Health Research, 15(9), 1277–1288.
annotation: Distinguishes conventional (inductive), directed (deductive), and summative content analysis. Cite to position your content-analysis approach.

apa: Blumer, H. (1954). What is wrong with social theory? American Sociological Review, 19(1), 3–10.
annotation: Origin of "sensitizing concepts." Cite when using loosely-defined theoretical concepts as analytic starting points.

apa: Stake, R. E. (1995). The art of case study research. Sage.
annotation: Interpretive/intrinsic case study. Cite for holistic, naturalistic case work.

apa: Yin, R. K. (2018). Case study research and applications: Design and methods (6th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The post-positivist case-study design tradition. Cite for propositions, multiple-case logic, and rigor.

apa: Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.
annotation: Education-friendly case study and general qualitative design. Cite in education contexts.

apa: Clandinin, D. J., & Connelly, F. M. (2000). Narrative inquiry: Experience and story in qualitative research. Jossey-Bass.
annotation: Founding text of narrative inquiry. Cite for experience-centered, story-based research.

apa: Riessman, C. K. (2008). Narrative methods for the human sciences. Sage.
annotation: Thematic, structural, and dialogic/performance narrative analysis. Cite for narrative analytic techniques.

apa: Smith, J. A., Flowers, P., & Larkin, M. (2022). Interpretative phenomenological analysis: Theory, method and research (2nd ed.). Sage.
annotation: The authoritative IPA manual. Cite for idiographic, experiential phenomenology.

apa: Ritchie, J., & Spencer, L. (1994). Qualitative data analysis for applied policy research. In A. Bryman & R. G. Burgess (Eds.), Analyzing qualitative data (pp. 173–194). Routledge.
annotation: Origin of Framework analysis. DOI applies to the edited volume. Cite for the matrix-based framework approach.

apa: Gale, N. K., Heath, G., Cameron, E., Rashid, S., & Redwood, S. (2013). Using the framework method for the analysis of qualitative data in multi-disciplinary health research. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 13, 117.
annotation: The widely-cited modern operationalization of Framework analysis. Cite for a team-based, stepwise procedure.

apa: Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The standard content-analysis methodology and home of Krippendorff's alpha. Cite for systematic content analysis.

apa: Brown, A. L. (1992). Design experiments: Theoretical and methodological challenges in creating complex interventions in classroom settings. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 2(2), 141–178.
annotation: Founding paper of design experiments. Cite for the origins of design-based research (DBR).

apa: Design-Based Research Collective. (2003). Design-based research: An emerging paradigm for educational inquiry. Educational Researcher, 32(1), 5–8.
annotation: The agenda-setting statement of DBR. Cite to define DBR.

apa: Barab, S., & Squire, K. (2004). Design-based research: Putting a stake in the ground. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(1), 1–14.
annotation: Influential framing of DBR's warrants. Cite for DBR's evidentiary claims.

apa: Collins, A., Joseph, D., & Bielaczyc, K. (2004). Design research: Theoretical and methodological issues. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(1), 15–42.
annotation: Methodological elaboration of design research. Cite for DBR methodology.

apa: Jordan, B., & Henderson, A. (1995). Interaction analysis: Foundations and practice. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 4(1), 39–103.
annotation: The foundational method for analyzing video records of interaction in the learning sciences. Cite for video/interaction analysis.

apa: American Educational Research Association. (2006). Standards for reporting on empirical social science research in AERA publications. Educational Researcher, 35(6), 33–40.
annotation: The AERA reporting standards. Cite for reporting expectations in education research.

apa: Ladson-Billings, G. (1995). Toward a theory of culturally relevant pedagogy. American Educational Research Journal, 32(3), 465–491.
annotation: Foundational culturally relevant framing. Cite for culturally relevant/responsive methodology in education.

apa: McDonald, N., Schoenebeck, S., & Forte, A. (2019). Reliability and inter-rater reliability in qualitative research: Norms and guidelines for CSCW and HCI practice. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 72, 1–23.
annotation: The definitive HCI/CSCW treatment of whether and when to use IRR; a meta-analysis finding IRR in ~1/9 of qualitative papers. Cite for reliability norms in HCI.

apa: Dourish, P. (2006). Implications for design. In Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '06) (pp. 541–550). ACM.
annotation: The classic critique of "implications for design" as the metric for ethnography in HCI. Cite on the value of ethnographic/theoretical contributions.

apa: Beyer, H., & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual design: Defining customer-centered systems. Morgan Kaufmann.
annotation: Source of contextual inquiry and affinity diagramming (the KJ-method lineage). Cite for affinity diagramming/contextual design.

apa: Muller, M. (2014). Curiosity, creativity, and surprise as analytic tools: Grounded theory method. In J. S. Olson & W. A. Kellogg (Eds.), Ways of knowing in HCI (pp. 25–48). Springer.
annotation: Grounded theory adapted for HCI. Cite for GTM in HCI.

apa: Furniss, D., Blandford, A., & Curzon, P. (2011). Confessions from a grounded theory PhD: Experiences and lessons learnt. In Proceedings of CHI 2011 (pp. 113–122). ACM.
annotation: A candid account of doing grounded theory in HCI. Cite for practical GTM guidance.

apa: Zimmerman, J., Forlizzi, J., & Evenson, S. (2007). Research through design as a method for interaction design research in HCI. In Proceedings of CHI '07 (pp. 493–502). ACM.
annotation: Established research through design (RtD) in HCI. Cite to frame design as inquiry.

apa: Gaver, W. (2012). What should we expect from research through design? In Proceedings of CHI '12 (pp. 937–946). ACM.
annotation: Influential argument on RtD's epistemology and rigor. Cite for RtD evaluation.

apa: Blandford, A., Furniss, D., & Makri, S. (2016). Qualitative HCI research: Going behind the scenes. Morgan & Claypool.
annotation: A practical synthesis of qualitative methods for HCI. Cite as an HCI-specific methods primer.

apa: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.
annotation: The original Cohen's kappa. Cite for chance-corrected agreement between two coders on nominal categories.

apa: Cohen, J. (1968). Weighted kappa: Nominal scale agreement with provision for scaled disagreement or partial credit. Psychological Bulletin, 70(4), 213–220.
annotation: Weighted kappa. Cite when disagreements differ in severity (ordered categories).

apa: Fleiss, J. L. (1971). Measuring nominal scale agreement among many raters. Psychological Bulletin, 76(5), 378–382.
annotation: Fleiss' kappa. Cite for 3+ raters where raters are not fixed across items.

apa: Scott, W. A. (1955). Reliability of content analysis: The case of nominal scale coding. Public Opinion Quarterly, 19(3), 321–325.
annotation: Scott's pi. Cite as the predecessor to kappa using a joint (rather than individual) chance distribution.

apa: Hayes, A. F., & Krippendorff, K. (2007). Answering the call for a standard reliability measure for coding data. Communication Methods and Measures, 1(1), 77–89.
annotation: The accessible standard reference for Krippendorff's alpha (any measurement level, ≥2 coders, missing data). Cite when you need one flexible coefficient.

apa: Feinstein, A. R., & Cicchetti, D. V. (1990). High agreement but low kappa: I. The problems of two paradoxes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 43(6), 543–549.
annotation: Defines the kappa paradox. Cite to explain why kappa can be low despite high observed agreement.

apa: Cicchetti, D. V., & Feinstein, A. R. (1990). High agreement but low kappa: II. Resolving the paradoxes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 43(6), 551–558.
annotation: The companion "resolution" paper. Cite for the recommended positive/negative agreement diagnostics.

apa: Gwet, K. L. (2008). Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 61(1), 29–48.
annotation: Introduces the AC1/AC2 statistics that resist the prevalence/paradox problem. Cite when prevalence is skewed.

apa: Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420–428.
annotation: The foundational ICC typology (six forms). Cite to choose an ICC model.

apa: McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30–46.
annotation: Extends and clarifies ICC inference. Cite alongside Shrout & Fleiss for ICC selection. (Correction in Psychological Methods, 1(4), 390.)

apa: Koo, T. K., & Li, M. Y. (2016). A guideline of selecting and reporting intraclass correlation coefficients for reliability research. Journal of Chiropractic Medicine, 15(2), 155–163.
annotation: The practical decision guide for the 10 ICC forms and interpretation bands. Cite for ICC selection and reporting.

apa: Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.
annotation: Source of the widely-used magnitude bands (Slight/Fair/Moderate/Substantial/Almost Perfect). Cite when interpreting kappa/alpha — but note the thresholds are explicitly arbitrary heuristics.

apa: Hallgren, K. A. (2012). Computing inter-rater reliability for observational data: An overview and tutorial. Tutorials in Quantitative Methods for Psychology, 8(1), 23–34.
annotation: A hands-on tutorial (with SPSS/R) for choosing and computing kappa and ICC. Cite for practical computation.

apa: O'Connor, C., & Joffe, H. (2020). Intercoder reliability in qualitative research: Debates and practical guidelines. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 19, 1–13.
annotation: Reviews the arguments for/against intercoder reliability and gives practical guidelines. Cite to decide whether ICR fits your study.

apa: Birt, L., Scott, S., Cavers, D., Campbell, C., & Walter, F. (2016). Member checking: A tool to enhance trustworthiness or merely a nod to validation? Qualitative Health Research, 26(13), 1802–1811.
annotation: Critical, practical treatment of member checking. Cite when designing respondent validation.

apa: Denzin, N. K. (2012). Triangulation 2.0. Journal of Mixed Methods Research, 6(2), 80–88.
annotation: Denzin's updated statement on triangulation. Cite for the concept's contemporary meaning.

apa: Guest, G., Bunce, A., & Johnson, L. (2006). How many interviews are enough? An experiment with data saturation and variability. Field Methods, 18(1), 59–82.
annotation: The most-cited empirical study of saturation; found saturation within the first twelve interviews. Cite for sample-size justification.

apa: Saunders, B., Sim, J., Kingstone, T., Baker, S., Waterfield, J., Bartlam, B., Burroughs, H., & Jinks, C. (2018). Saturation in qualitative research: Exploring its conceptualization and operationalization. Quality & Quantity, 52(4), 1893–1907.
annotation: Clarifies competing meanings of saturation. Cite to specify which saturation you mean.

apa: Malterud, K., Siersma, V. D., & Guassora, A. D. (2016). Sample size in qualitative interview studies: Guided by information power. Qualitative Health Research, 26(13), 1753–1760.
annotation: Proposes "information power" as an alternative to saturation. Cite for a more defensible sample-size rationale.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2021). To saturate or not to saturate? Questioning data saturation as a useful concept for thematic analysis and sample-size rationales. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 13(2), 201–216.
annotation: The reflexive-TA critique of saturation. Cite when rejecting saturation logic in interpretivist work.

apa: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. (1979). The Belmont Report: Ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research. U.S. Department of Health & Human Services.
annotation: The foundational U.S. statement of research ethics — respect for persons, beneficence, justice. Cite for the principles underlying IRB review.

apa: Brandt, A. M. (1978). Racism and research: The case of the Tuskegee syphilis study. The Hastings Center Report, 8(6), 21–29.
annotation: The definitive scholarly account of the Tuskegee study and its ethical failures. Cite when invoking Tuskegee as motivation for human-subjects protections.

apa: Chambers, C. D., & Tzavella, L. (2022). The past, present and future of Registered Reports. Nature Human Behaviour, 6(1), 29–42.
annotation: The definitive overview of Registered Reports, where a study is peer-reviewed and accepted on its question and design before any data are collected. Cite for the principle that a study should be worth doing regardless of how the results turn out.

apa: Nosek, B. A., Ebersole, C. R., DeHaven, A. C., & Mellor, D. T. (2018). The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(11), 2600–2606.
annotation: Argues for committing hypotheses and an analysis plan in advance to keep confirmatory and exploratory work distinct. Cite when teaching students to write the analysis plan before collecting data.

apa: Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs—Principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134–2156.
annotation: How to actually integrate qualitative and quantitative strands—connecting, building, merging, and joint displays—rather than reporting them side by side. Cite for why a joint display yields a takeaway (confirmation, expansion, or discordance) regardless of the statistical result.

apa: McCauley, R., Fitzgerald, S., Lewandowski, G., Murphy, L., Simon, B., Thomas, L., & Zander, C. (2008). Debugging: A review of the literature from an educational perspective. Computer Science Education, 18(2), 67–92.
annotation: A review synthesizing decades of debugging-education research — a good 'anchor tome' to read deeply and snowball from. Cite as the map of the debugging-education area.

apa: Fitzgerald, S., Lewandowski, G., McCauley, R., Murphy, L., Simon, B., Thomas, L., & Zander, C. (2008). Debugging: Finding, fixing and flailing, a multi-institutional study of novice debuggers. Computer Science Education, 18(2), 93–116.
annotation: Multi-institution study of how novices actually debug (often 'flailing' without a plan). Cite for evidence on novice debugging behavior; a natural snowball from McCauley et al.

apa: Loksa, D., Ko, A. J., Jernigan, W., Oleson, A., Mendez, C. J., & Burnett, M. M. (2016). Programming, problem solving, and self-awareness: Effects of explicit guidance. In Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 1449–1461). Association for Computing Machinery.
annotation: Explicit metacognitive guidance improves novices' programming problem-solving. Cite as the basis for a metacognitive-prompt intervention.

apa: Aleven, V., Stahl, E., Schworm, S., Fischer, F., & Wallace, R. (2003). Help seeking and help design in interactive learning environments. Review of Educational Research, 73(3), 277–320.
annotation: Foundational review of help-seeking in tutoring systems — help offered is not the same as help used. Cite as an adjacent-domain analogy for CS help-seeking.

apa: Karabenick, S. A., & Newman, R. S. (Eds.). (2006). Help seeking in academic settings: Goals, groups, and contexts. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
annotation: Anchor volume on academic help-seeking as a self-regulated learning strategy (help avoidance as a threat response). Cite for the motivation-psychology framing of help-seeking.

apa: Sanders, K., Sheard, J., Becker, B. A., Eckerdal, A., Hamouda, S., & Simon. (2019). Inferential statistics in computing education research: A methodological review. Proceedings of ICER '19, 177–185.
annotation: Reviewed 14 years of ICER: the field's 'big three' are the t-test, chi-squared, and Mann-Whitney, with frequent reporting flaws (missing df, effect sizes, assumption checks). Cite for what CER uses and gets wrong.

apa: Randolph, J. J., Julnes, G., Sutinen, E., & Lehman, S. (2008). A methodological review of computer science education research. Journal of Information Technology Education: Research, 7, 135–162.
annotation: 352 CER articles, 2000–2005: one-group posttest-only was the modal design, 38% of human-participant papers offered only anecdotal evidence, 86% convenience sampling. Cite when motivating comparison groups and honest sampling claims.

apa: Guerzhoy, M. (2023). "Medium-n studies" in computing education conferences. Koli Calling '23.
annotation: Class-sized samples are usually too small to detect typical effects; computing p-values for underpowered studies misleads. Cite in the power discussion.

apa: Robertson, J. (2012). Likert-type scales, statistical methods, and effect sizes. Communications of the ACM, 55(5), 6–7.
annotation: Short CACM piece on ordinal data mistreatment and missing effect sizes in HCI/CS venues. Cite for the Likert-as-interval problem.

apa: Kaptein, M. C., Nass, C., & Markopoulos, P. (2010). Powerful and consistent analysis of Likert-type rating scales. Proceedings of CHI '10, 2391–2394.
annotation: 45% of CHI papers used Likert-type data but only 8% used non-parametric analysis. Cite for the scale of the ordinal-data problem.

apa: Sanders, K., Vahrenhold, J., & McCartney, R. (2023). How do computing education researchers talk about threats and limitations? Proceedings of ICER '23.
annotation: Maps how CER papers discuss limitations onto internal/external/construct/statistical-conclusion validity. Cite when teaching limitations writing.

apa: Heckman, S., Carver, J. C., Sherriff, M., & Al-Zubidy, A. (2022). A systematic literature review of empiricism and norms of reporting in computing education research literature. ACM Transactions on Computing Education, 22(1), Article 3.
annotation: 427 papers: reporting gaps (missing RQs, participants, design details) block replication and meta-analysis. Cite for reporting norms.

apa: Ihantola, P., Vihavainen, A., Ahadi, A., et al. (2015). Educational data mining and learning analytics in programming: Literature review and case studies. ITiCSE-WGR '15, 41–63.
annotation: The canonical EDM/LA-in-programming review. Cite as the further-reading pointer for what this module deliberately leaves out.

apa: Porter, L., Bailey Lee, C., & Simon, B. (2013). Halving fail rates using peer instruction: A study of four computer science courses. Proceedings of SIGCSE '13, 177–182.
annotation: Exemplar multi-course quasi-experiment with a large, practically meaningful effect. Cite as a design model.

apa: Michaeli, T., & Romeike, R. (2019). Improving debugging skills in the classroom: The effects of teaching a systematic debugging process. Proceedings of WiPSCE '19.
annotation: Quasi-experiment: explicit systematic-debugging instruction improved debugging performance and self-efficacy. The real-world twin of this module's running example.

apa: Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). Regression and other stories. Cambridge University Press.
annotation: The modeling spine for lessons 7–10: regression as comparison, the divide-by-4 rule, multilevel thinking. Free PDF and code examples at the companion site.

apa: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: A practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, 863.
annotation: The practical effect-size primer: which d, which eta-squared, and how to report them. Open access.

apa: Appelbaum, M., Cooper, H., Kline, R. B., Mayo-Wilson, E., Nezu, A. M., & Rao, S. M. (2018). Journal article reporting standards for quantitative research in psychology: The APA Publications and Communications Board task force report. American Psychologist, 73(1), 3–25.
annotation: JARS-Quant: what a quantitative report must contain. Cite for the reporting checklist.

apa: Wasserstein, R. L., Schirm, A. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2019). Moving to a world beyond "p < 0.05". The American Statistician, 73(sup1), 1–19.
annotation: The ASA-adjacent editorial on retiring bright-line significance. Cite for estimation-first framing.

apa: Norton, E. C., Dowd, B. E., & Maciejewski, M. L. (2018). Odds ratios—current best practice and use. JAMA, 320(1), 84–85.
annotation: Why odds ratios mislead when outcomes are common and why marginal effects communicate better. The core citation for the logistic-translation lesson.

apa: Mize, T. D. (2019). Best practices for estimating, interpreting, and presenting nonlinear interaction effects. Sociological Science, 6, 81–117.
annotation: Predicted probabilities and marginal effects for nonlinear models, with worked figures. Open access.

apa: Arel-Bundock, V., Greifer, N., & Heiss, A. (2024). How to interpret statistical models using marginaleffects for R and Python. Journal of Statistical Software, 111(9), 1–32.
annotation: The marginaleffects package paper — predictions, comparisons, slopes in both R and Python. Cite next to any AME code.

apa: McNeish, D., Stapleton, L. M., & Silverman, R. D. (2017). On the unnecessary ubiquity of hierarchical linear modeling. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 114–140.
annotation: MLM is not the only fix for clustering: cluster-robust errors and GEE answer different questions. The backbone of the clustered-data lesson's model choice.

apa: Theobald, E. (2018). Students are rarely independent: When, why, and how to use random effects in discipline-based education research. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 17(3), rm2.
annotation: The audience-matched multilevel-models reading: nesting in classroom data and what to do about it. Open access.

apa: Hubbard, A. E., Ahern, J., Fleischer, N. L., et al. (2010). To GEE or not to GEE: Comparing population average and mixed models for estimating the associations between neighborhood risk factors and health. Epidemiology, 21(4), 467–474.
annotation: The readable GEE-vs-mixed-models comparison: marginal vs conditional estimands. Cite when choosing between them.

apa: McNeish, D. M., & Stapleton, L. M. (2016). Modeling clustered data with very few clusters. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(4), 495–518.
annotation: What breaks when you have a handful of clusters and which small-sample corrections help. Cite for the two-sections honesty beat.

apa: Mancl, L. A., & DeRouen, T. A. (2001). A covariance estimator for GEE with improved small-sample properties. Biometrics, 57(1), 126–134.
annotation: The standard small-sample sandwich correction for GEE. Cite when clusters number in the dozens.

apa: Sommet, N., & Morselli, D. (2017). Keep calm and learn multilevel logistic modeling: A simplified three-step procedure using Stata, R, Mplus, and SPSS. International Review of Social Psychology, 30(1), 203–218.
annotation: Step-by-step multilevel logistic walkthrough with code in four packages. Open access.

apa: Kline, R. B. (2023). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (5th ed.). Guilford Press.
annotation: The standard SEM textbook: specification, identification, estimation, fit. Cite as the depth reference behind the SEM lesson.

apa: Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(2), 1–36.
annotation: The lavaan paper — cite next to any lavaan syntax.

apa: Hu, L., & Bentler, P. M. (1999). Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis: Conventional criteria versus new alternatives. Structural Equation Modeling, 6(1), 1–55.
annotation: Source of the CFI ≥ .95 / RMSEA ≤ .06 conventions. Cite it — and cite Marsh et al. (2004) beside it.

apa: Marsh, H. W., Hau, K.-T., & Wen, Z. (2004). In search of golden rules: Comment on hypothesis-testing approaches to setting cutoff values for fit indexes and dangers in overgeneralizing Hu and Bentler's (1999) findings. Structural Equation Modeling, 11(3), 320–341.
annotation: Why the fit-index cutoffs are not golden rules. Always pair with Hu & Bentler.

apa: Hoekstra, R., Kiers, H. A. L., & Johnson, A. (2012). Are assumptions of well-known statistical techniques checked, and why (not)? Frontiers in Psychology, 3, 137.
annotation: Researchers rarely check assumptions, and preliminary normality tests are a poor ritual. Cite in the assumptions discussion.

apa: Lord, F. M. (1967). A paradox in the interpretation of group comparisons. Psychological Bulletin, 68(5), 304–305.
annotation: Lord's paradox: with intact groups, covariate adjustment and change scores can disagree. Cite in the pre/post walkthrough.

apa: Van Breukelen, G. J. P. (2006). ANCOVA versus change from baseline had more power in randomized studies and more bias in nonrandomized studies. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 59(9), 920–925.
annotation: ANCOVA vs gain scores, by design type. Cite alongside Lord (1967).

apa: GAISE College Report ASA Revision Committee. (2016). Guidelines for assessment and instruction in statistics education (GAISE) college report 2016. American Statistical Association.
annotation: Statistics-education consensus guidelines: teach statistics as investigation, foster multivariable thinking. Free.

apa: Lindeløv, J. K. (2019). Common statistical tests are linear models (or: how to teach stats). Online resource.
annotation: One page showing t-tests, ANOVA, and correlations as linear models — the unity move the regression lesson makes. Free.

apa: Fincher, S. A., & Robins, A. V. (Eds.). (2019). The Cambridge handbook of computing education research. Cambridge University Press.
annotation: The field handbook; chapters 5–6 (Haden) cover descriptive and inferential statistics for CER. Cite as the general methods reference.

apa: American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education. (2014). Standards for educational and psychological testing. AERA.
annotation: The authority on validity and fairness: five sources of validity evidence. The measurement block's constitution.

apa: Messick, S. (1995). Validity of psychological assessment: Validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning. American Psychologist, 50(9), 741–749.
annotation: The unified view of construct validity. Cite for validity-as-one-thing.

apa: Kane, M. T. (2013). Validating the interpretations and uses of test scores. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(1), 1–73.
annotation: The argument-based approach: validity is an argument for an interpretation and use, not a property of a test.

apa: Reeves, T. D., & Marbach-Ad, G. (2016). Contemporary test validity in theory and practice: A primer for discipline-based education researchers. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 15(1), rm1.
annotation: The best audience-matched validity reading: modern validity theory written for discipline-based education researchers. Open access.

apa: Sijtsma, K. (2009). On the use, the misuse, and the very limited usefulness of Cronbach's alpha. Psychometrika, 74(1), 107–120.
annotation: Alpha does not measure unidimensionality and is routinely misused. Cite when introducing omega.

apa: McNeish, D. (2018). Thanks coefficient alpha, we'll take it from here. Psychological Methods, 23(3), 412–433.
annotation: The alpha-to-omega argument in full. Cite for the modern default.

apa: Boateng, G. O., Neilands, T. B., Frongillo, E. A., Melgar-Quiñonez, H. R., & Young, S. L. (2018). Best practices for developing and validating scales for health, social, and behavioral research: A primer. Frontiers in Public Health, 6, 149.
annotation: The checklist-style scale-development pipeline the instrument lesson follows. Open access.

apa: DeVellis, R. F., & Thorpe, C. T. (2022). Scale development: Theory and applications (5th ed.). SAGE.
annotation: The survey-scale bible: item writing, response formats, reduction. Depth reference for scale building.

apa: Bandalos, D. L. (2018). Measurement theory and applications for the social sciences. Guilford Press.
annotation: The single-volume spine of the measurement block: CTT, reliability, validity, EFA/CFA, IRT, DIF, equating.

apa: de Ayala, R. J. (2022). The theory and practice of item response theory (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.
annotation: The IRT reference, model by model with software output. Cite for parameter estimation detail and sample-size demands.

apa: Embretson, S. E., & Reise, S. P. (2000). Item response theory for psychologists. Lawrence Erlbaum.
annotation: The most readable conceptual IRT book — the 'new rules of measurement' framing the why-IRT lesson uses.

apa: Baker, F. B. (2001). The basics of item response theory (2nd ed.). ERIC Clearinghouse on Assessment and Evaluation.
annotation: Free, gentle, ICC-first introduction to IRT — the on-ramp reading for the IRT lessons.

apa: Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory package for the R environment. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(6), 1–29.
annotation: The mirt paper — cite next to any mirt code.

apa: Wilson, M. (2023). Constructing measures: An item response modeling approach (2nd ed.). Routledge.
annotation: Construct-map-driven instrument development (the BEAR Assessment System). The instrument lesson's design spine alongside Boateng.

apa: Adams, W. K., & Wieman, C. E. (2011). Development and validation of instruments to measure learning of expert-like thinking. International Journal of Science Education, 33(9), 1289–1312.
annotation: DBER instrument development end to end, from interviews to validation. Cite as the discipline-based model.

apa: Willis, G. B., & Artino, A. R. (2013). What do our respondents think we're asking? Using cognitive interviewing to improve medical education surveys. Journal of Graduate Medical Education, 5(3), 353–356.
annotation: Short, free cognitive-interviewing primer for item validation. Open access.

apa: Boone, W. J. (2016). Rasch analysis for instrument development: Why, when, and how? CBE—Life Sciences Education, 15(4), rm4.
annotation: Rasch for instrument developers, written for education researchers. Open access; pair with Planinic et al.

apa: Planinic, M., Boone, W. J., Susac, A., & Ivanjek, L. (2019). Rasch analysis in physics education research: Why measurement matters. Physical Review Physics Education Research, 15(2), 020111.
annotation: Worked Rasch analyses in a sister DBER field. Open access.

apa: Bloch, R., & Norman, G. (2012). Generalizability theory for the perplexed: A practical introduction and guide: AMEE Guide No. 68. Medical Teacher, 34(11), 960–992.
annotation: The one G-theory pointer: what it adds beyond alpha when raters and tasks both vary.

apa: Linacre, J. M. (1994). Sample size and item calibration stability. Rasch Measurement Transactions, 7(4), 328.
annotation: The much-cited Rasch sample-size guidance (~100–250 for stable calibration). Cite in the model-choice discussion.

apa: Kolen, M. J., & Brennan, R. L. (2014). Test equating, scaling, and linking: Methods and practices (3rd ed.). Springer.
annotation: The equating reference — cited as a pointer, not a reading; pre/post with overlapping items is secretly an equating problem.

apa: Tew, A. E., & Guzdial, M. (2011). The FCS1: A language independent assessment of CS1 knowledge. Proceedings of SIGCSE '11, 111–116.
annotation: The original language-independent CS1 assessment. Never publicly released — which motivated the SCS1.

apa: Parker, M. C., Guzdial, M., & Engleman, S. (2016). Replication, validation, and use of a language independent CS1 knowledge assessment. Proceedings of ICER '16, 93–101.
annotation: The SCS1 — the CS1 knowledge assessment the instruments lesson's arc is built on.

apa: Xie, B., Davidson, M. J., Li, M., & Ko, A. J. (2019). An item response theory evaluation of a language-independent CS1 knowledge assessment. Proceedings of SIGCSE '19, 699–705.
annotation: IRT re-analysis of the SCS1: some items measure a different construct, several are too hard. The model of re-examining a 'validated' instrument.

apa: Davidson, M. J., Wortzman, B., Ko, A. J., & Li, M. (2021). Investigating item bias in a CS1 exam with differential item functioning. Proceedings of SIGCSE '21, 1142–1148.
annotation: Gender DIF found in an SCS1-derived exam: item-level bias hiding inside an acceptable total score. The DIF lesson's central case.

apa: Parker, M. C., Guzdial, M., & Tew, A. E. (2021). Uses, revisions, and the future of validated assessments in computing education: A case study of the FCS1 and SCS1. Proceedings of ICER '21.
annotation: A decade of ad-hoc shortening, subsetting, and translating the SCS1 — and why each invalidates the original validity argument. The reuse cautionary tale.

apa: Vieira, C., Vásquez, M. F., Meza, F., Quintero-Manes, A., & Godoy, D. (2024). Identifying difficult questions and student difficulties in a Spanish version of a programming assessment instrument (SCS1). ACM Transactions on Computing Education.
annotation: Translation is adaptation: think-alouds revealed the Spanish SCS1 behaves differently. Cross-language validity evidence does not transfer for free.

apa: Porter, L., Zingaro, D., Liao, S. N., Taylor, C., Webb, K. C., Lee, C., & Clancy, M. (2019). BDSI: A validated concept inventory for basic data structures. Proceedings of ICER '19, 111–119.
annotation: Gold-standard concept-inventory process: faculty Delphi, 100+ student interviews, iterative drafts, statistical evaluation.

apa: Hamouda, S., Edwards, S. H., Elmongui, H. G., Ernst, J. V., & Shaffer, C. A. (2017). A basic recursion concept inventory. Computer Science Education, 27(2), 121–148.
annotation: Misconception-driven concept-inventory development — Virginia Tech work. The local model for the DCI running example.

apa: Dorn, B., & Tew, A. E. (2015). Empirical validation and application of the computing attitudes survey. Computer Science Education, 25(1), 1–36.
annotation: Full re-validation of an attitude survey adapted from physics — the model for adapting affective instruments across disciplines.

apa: Ramalingam, V., & Wiedenbeck, S. (1998). Development and validation of scores on a computer programming self-efficacy scale and group analyses of novice programmer self-efficacy. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 19(4), 367–381.
annotation: The classic programming self-efficacy scale most later CS self-efficacy work adapts.

apa: Tsai, M.-J., Wang, C.-Y., & Hsu, P.-F. (2019). Developing the computer programming self-efficacy scale for computer literacy education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 56(8), 1345–1360.
annotation: Programming self-efficacy scale with a Debug subscale — the closest thing to a validated debugging self-efficacy measure.

apa: Yang, Y., Baird, A., O'Rourke, E., Brennan, K., & Schneider, B. (2024). Decoding debugging instruction: A systematic literature review of debugging interventions. ACM Transactions on Computing Education.
annotation: Systematic review of debugging interventions 2010–2022: outcome measures are almost all ad hoc — there is no accepted validated debugging assessment. The DCI's reason to exist.

apa: Decker, A., & McGill, M. M. (2019). A topical review of evaluation instruments for computing education. Proceedings of SIGCSE '19, 558–564.
annotation: The instrument-landscape review behind csedresearch.org — search there before building your own.

apa: Finnie-Ansley, J., Denny, P., Becker, B. A., Luxton-Reilly, A., & Prather, J. (2022). The robots are coming: Exploring the implications of OpenAI Codex on introductory programming. Proceedings of ACE '22, 10–19.
annotation: Codex outscored most CS1 students on exam questions. The opening evidence for the assessment-contamination warning.

apa: Savelka, J., Agarwal, A., Bogart, C., Song, Y., & Sakr, M. (2023). Can generative pre-trained transformers (GPT) pass assessments in higher education programming courses? Proceedings of ITiCSE '23.
annotation: GPT models passing programming-course assessments — unproctored instruments can no longer separate student ability from AI assistance.

apa: Küchemann, S., Steinert, S., Kuhn, J., Avila, K., & Ruzika, S. (2024). Large language models—valid tools for concept inventory item generation? Reliability and validity of concept inventory items generated by ChatGPT. Frontiers in Psychology, 15, 1426209.
annotation: LLM-drafted concept-inventory items approach — but do not equal — human quality; expert review stays mandatory.

apa: MacNeil, S., Denny, P., Tran, A., Leinonen, J., Bernstein, S., & Hellas, A. (2024). Imagining computing education assessment after generative AI. arXiv:2401.04601.
annotation: What assessment design can still mean when models solve the items. Cite in the contamination discussion.

apa: Prather, J., Denny, P., Leinonen, J., et al. (2023). The robots are here: Navigating the generative AI revolution in computing education. ITiCSE-WGR '23.
annotation: The ITiCSE working-group survey of GenAI in computing education — the field's orientation document.

apa: Association for Computing Machinery. (2023). ACM policy on authorship: Frequently asked questions (generative AI provisions).
annotation: ACM's rules: generative AI cannot be an author; use must be disclosed in Acknowledgements; confidential material must not be uploaded.

apa: American Psychological Association. (2023). APA Journals policy on generative AI: Additional guidance.
annotation: APA's disclosure rules: report GenAI use in Method, cite the tool, AI is never an author.

apa: McAdoo, T. (2023). How to cite ChatGPT. APA Style Blog.
annotation: The APA Style mechanics for citing LLM output.

apa: Virginia Tech Division of Scholarly Integrity and Research Compliance. (2023). Guidance: Using artificial intelligence during research activities.
annotation: The lab's own institution on AI in research: participant data, confidentiality, and reviewer obligations. Read before any AI use touching study data.

apa: Virginia Tech Division of IT. (2025). Be judicious when sharing university data with publicly available AI tools.
annotation: VT's data-sharing notice: which tools are approved for university data and which are not.

apa: Privacy Technical Assistance Center, U.S. Department of Education. (2013). Data de-identification: An overview of basic terms.
annotation: FERPA-adjacent de-identification: indirect identifiers and small cells count. 'I deleted the names' is not de-identified.

apa: U.S. National Science Foundation. (2023). Notice to the research community: Use of generative artificial intelligence technology in the NSF merit review process.
annotation: NSF prohibits uploading proposals under review to non-approved GenAI tools. Reviewer confidentiality extends to AI.

apa: National Institutes of Health. (2023). The use of generative artificial intelligence technologies is prohibited for the NIH peer review process (NOT-OD-23-149).
annotation: NIH's parallel prohibition for peer review.

apa: Walters, W. H., & Wilder, E. I. (2023). Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Scientific Reports, 13, 14045.
annotation: Measured citation fabrication: a large share of GPT-generated references are invented, often pairing real authors with fake titles.

apa: Chelli, M., Descamps, J., Lavoué, V., et al. (2024). Hallucination rates and reference accuracy of ChatGPT and Bard for systematic reviews: Comparative analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 26, e53164.
annotation: Hallucination rates for LLM-suggested references in systematic-review tasks. Never cite what you have not retrieved.

apa: Kabir, S., Udo-Imeh, D. N., Kou, B., & Zhang, T. (2024). Is Stack Overflow obsolete? An empirical study of the characteristics of ChatGPT answers to Stack Overflow questions. Proceedings of CHI '24.
annotation: About half of ChatGPT programming answers contained errors — and readers overlooked them ~39% of the time. Rerun everything.

apa: Ruta, M., et al. (2025). ChatGPT for univariate statistics: Validation of AI-assisted data analysis in healthcare research. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 27, e63550.
annotation: Prompt specificity moved LLM statistical-analysis accuracy from 32.5% to 92.5%. The evidence behind schema-first prompting.

apa: Chhikara, P. (2025). Mind the confidence gap: Overconfidence, calibration, and distractor effects in large language models. arXiv:2502.11028.
annotation: Models state high confidence while being wrong — stated confidence is not evidence.

apa: Dobler, C. C., et al. (2025). ChatGPT as a tool for biostatisticians: A tutorial on applications, opportunities, and pitfalls. Statistics in Medicine.
annotation: A statistician's-eye tutorial: where LLMs help with analysis and where competence remains the prerequisite.

apa: Smith, A. M., et al. (2024). Ten simple rules for using large language models in science. PLOS Computational Biology, 20(1), e1011767.
annotation: The compact rules-of-engagement paper for LLMs in research workflows.

apa: Perkel, J. M. (2023). Six tips for better coding with ChatGPT. Nature, 618, 422–423.
annotation: Practical LLM-assisted coding habits: small steps, tests, verification.

apa: Glynn, A. (2024). Academ-AI: Documenting the undisclosed use of generative artificial intelligence in academic publishing. arXiv:2411.15218.
annotation: Undisclosed LLM use is being actively detected and catalogued in published papers. Disclose.
